title: Edwin and Morcar, the Earls of Mercia and Northumberland
description: William Mason's first tragedy, written while he was still a young man in the north and played in London in the spring of his debut season. Its claim on literary history is less its plot than its metre: it is one of the first English tragedies of the mid century to be written throughout in blank (unrhymed) verse, at a time when the critics of the 'just rules' still treated rhyme as the polite default of the stage. The subject is drawn from the period of the Danish conquest of England, and the two titular earls are offered as native, Saxon virtue under pressure from a foreign invader.
plot_or_argument: The action turns on the Danish invasion of England and on the obligation of the great northern and midland earls to resist it while maintaining their honour at a hostile court. Edwin and Morcar are placed between the demands of patriotic resistance and the private ties of affection and friendship, so that the political crisis tests personal loyalty as much as it tests arms. As befits an early work by a poet more thoughtful than clever, the intrigue is relatively plain and the interest is carried by declarations of virtue, of friendship and of national spirit. The play's real argument is made in its preface and in its practice: that English tragedy should recover the 'native and sublime' dignity of unrhymed measure rather than submit to the tunnery of couplets.
narrative_structure: A regular five-act tragedy in the neo-classical arrangement, with the political and amatory plots running in parallel and resolved by the close; the printed edition is preceded by dedication and prefatory matter in which the author defends his choice of measure.
principal_characters: Edwin, Earl of Mercia; Morcar, Earl of Northumberland
literary_form: Tragedy for the London stage, printed in the ordinary acting edition format with dramatis personae; regular acts; sustained blank verse dialogue with sententious declamation.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse: unrhymed iambic pentameter, end-stopped and carefully accented, in the deliberate, 'meditated' manner Mason preferred, without the running enjambment of the later Shakespearean revivals.
historical_context: It belongs to the 1740s efflorescence of British and Saxon subjects on the stage and to the contemporaneous quarrel over rhyme in dramatic verse, in which Joseph Warton and the editors of periodical reviews pressed the case for blank measure while neoclassical judges thought it harsh. Mason, a country clergyman and then a tutor, wrote as an amateur in the respectable sense, and his success encouraged the same blank-verse tragic experiment he pursued again in Caractacus.
literary_significance: It is a landmark in the reinstatement of blank verse on the English stage, a development that runs from this play through Mason's Caractacus and the Shakespeare revivals of the 1740s and 1760s to the tragedies of the following generation. Its Saxon-patriotic matter also feeds the mid-century vogue for a native, 'British' antiquity as a source of moral and theatrical sublimity.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the play was published with Mason's name and its authorship was never in doubt. The date of composition is not fixed by the surviving evidence and is left null rather than estimated.
bibliographical_notes: First acted and first printed in 1747; the exact composition years are not asserted here. The edition used for this record is the first London octavo of the year of publication; no printer is claimed beyond the 1747 imprint.

title: Caractacus: A Dramatic Poem
description: Mason's most admired tragedy, and a work he labelled a 'dramatic poem' rather than a play, partly because it was written for a circle of subscribers and for the reader's theatre as much as for the pit. Its subject is the British chief Caractacus, defeated by Rome, carried in chains to Italy and displayed in triumph before the emperor, and there outdoing his captors in the dignity with which he speaks of liberty and of his country. The machinery of Druids and of British superstition gives the poem its religious and sublimer colour.
plot_or_argument: The action is built on the collision between Roman imperial splendour and captive British virtue. Caractacus, having lost his kingdom in the field, keeps his sovereignty in the language he uses at Rome, refusing the concessions that would make his captivity comfortable. Around him the poem arranges the expected attachments of love and friendship, and the Druidic element supplies prophecy, sacred grove and solemn rite, all of which Mason treats as a national priesthood of great moral elevation. The dramatic interest is thereby concentrated not in the plot but in the set-piece of the conquered man before the conqueror, where the language of liberty is spoken with a force the contemporary reader recognised as the sublimity of unrhymed verse achieved.
narrative_structure: A five-act dramatic poem whose movement is episodic rather than tightly plotted, rising to the Roman triumph and the audience with the emperor as its rhetorical centre.
principal_characters: Caractacus; the Druids of the British grove; the court of the emperor Claudius at Rome
literary_form: Dramatic poem / closet tragedy with a strong lyrical and descriptive element; regular acts; printed with prefatory and dedicatory matter and with the author's account of the subject's sources.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of a carefully modulated kind, with short sententious lines for declamation and longer, more rhythmic periods for the Druidical and descriptive passages; Mason's practice here was commonly cited by later editors of the blank-verse controversy as evidence that unrhymed measure could be made 'musical'.
historical_context: Published in the year after the fall of Quebec, when British patriotic feeling and the cult of ancient 'British' liberty were unusually available to a poet, and in the middle of the critical debate about dramatic measure. Mason composed it largely in private and issued it by subscription, a publishing route that let a clergyman-poet keep the dignity of the work independent of theatrical managers.
literary_significance: For decades it was the standard example of modern English blank verse and of the patriotic 'British' subject treated in elevated measure, and it was praised for exactly that by later critics of the poetical revival. It also became a schoolroom and elocutionary text, and its Druidical machinery is a notable stage in the eighteenth-century imaginative recovery of the Celtic past.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem carries Mason's name in the first edition and its making is documented in his correspondence and in his later collected edition. Its first stage representation, whenever it came, is not asserted here.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1759 as 'Caractacus: A Dramatic Poem'; it was subsequently adapted for the London stage in the following decade, and Mason revised the text for his collected poems. The precise date of its first theatrical performance is uncertain and is therefore recorded as null.

title: The English Garden
description: Mason's didactic poem on the theory and practice of the 'improved' English pleasure ground, and one of the two or three most influential verses ever written on garden design. It defends the modern irregular style against the geometry of the formal garden, and it treats the lay of ground, the concealment of boundaries, the planting of belts and clumps, water, and the disposition of buildings as matters at once of taste and of moral feeling.
plot_or_argument: The poem proceeds by precept and illustration rather than by action. It surveys what the English garden had become since the reaction against the formal line, argues that its improvements should follow the 'genius' of the place rather than an imported pattern, and cautions the possessor against excess: against too much art betraying itself, against costly ornament, and against the petty tyrannies of the landscape contractor. The picturesque vocabulary of the age is translated into practical instruction, with the Chinese garden and the paintings of Claude and Salvator offered as models of composition. Throughout, the retired ground is made a figure of a well-ordered mind, so that the instruction in planting is also an argument about retirement, virtue and national taste.
narrative_structure: A preceptive didactic poem organised into books, each handling its own department of the subject, with descriptive digression and historical survey running inside the framework of instruction.
literary_form: Didactic poem in the Thomson school, in books, with descriptive and reflective passages embedded in the preceptive argument; related separately to his essay on topiary, here treated under the name of 'green sculpture'.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter) of close, weighted and frequently epigrammatic texture, with a strongly marked caesura and a preference for the balanced period; the manner is deliberately that of Thomson's 'The Seasons' adapted to instruction.
historical_context: It appears at the moment when the English landscape garden had become a national institution and a subject of open argument, between the practical doctrines of 'Capability' Brown and the more picturesque, varied taste urged by Uvedale Price's generation. Mason wrote as an amateur of gardens with a rector's income, and his poem addresses the country gentleman at a time when estate improvement and the language of taste were becoming a single conversation.
literary_significance: It fixed in verse the vocabulary of the improved garden and handed it on to the debate of the 1790s between the picturesque and the 'beautiful' garden, in which Price and Knight were still answering positions already stated here. As a document of the eighteenth-century marriage of ethics and landscape, it is the most substantial estate poem of the third quarter of the century.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Mason's name is on the first edition and he later reprinted the poem in his collected works. The years of composition are not precisely determinable and are left null.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1768, in books, and reissued in Mason's collected 'Poems' with revisions and with his annotations. The separate 'green sculpture' essay is a companion piece of the same period; its exact first-print details are not asserted here.

title: The Grave
description: Robert Blair's meditation on death, buried bodies and the resurrection, the poem that gave the graveyard school its name and its characteristic atmosphere. It is written in a heavy, sonorous blank verse and moves through the churchyard, the coffin, the worm and the general dissolution, turning the contemplation of putrefaction into an argument for immortality. It is also a work of the devotional edge of the Augustan age: Blair was a friend and fellow-minister of the evangelical circle around Ralph Cudworth the younger, and the poem's religious weight is not merely decorative.
plot_or_argument: There is no story, only the sustained exercise of a single thought. The speaker first dwells on the physical facts of burial and decay with a candour that the age found almost indecent, and describes the churchyard at night as the place where these facts are most visibly assembled. From the darkness of the grave the poem argues upward: the same dissolution which appals the unbelief of the worldling is for the believer the avenue to a resurrection, and the dead body becomes a 'seed' committed to the ground. The meditations on the last judgment, on the sleep of the dead and on the triumph of the living over the grave are the poem's true conclusion, and they justify its terrible preliminary imagery. Its characteristic mixture of horror and hope is what later readers of the 1740s and 1790s recognised as a new seriousness in English verse.
narrative_structure: A continuous meditative argument in a single voice, loosely articulated in sections following the progress of thought from the churchyard and the coffin to the resurrection and the last day; no dramatis personae and no narrative.
literary_form: Meditative blank-verse poem in the continuation of the 'Night Thoughts' tradition of the 1740s; descriptive and declamatory passages alternate with direct address and apostrophe; passages were afterward used as hymns and as anthology pieces.
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of great weight and latinity, with long suspended syntax, repeated keywords and a deliberate harshness of sound which contemporaries admired as sublimity and others censured as inflation.
historical_context: It belongs to the religious current running under Augustan neoclassicism: the evangelical revival of the 1730s and 1740s, Blair's friendship with the ministers of the London 'British' Presbyterian meeting, and the vogue for poems upon the last things which produced Parnell's and Young's meditations and Gray's early essays in terror. It was published in the decade of the 'graveyard' imagination and soon associated with an engraving design by William Hogarth.
literary_significance: It is the founding text of what later historians have called the Graveyard School, and its title gave the group its name. Its blend of physical realism about death with evangelical hope marks the transition from Augustan meditation to the preromantic taste for terror, and it shaped the devotional and funereal vocabulary of Gray, of Blair's Irish and Scottish successors and of the Gothic romance of the following generation.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested: published anonymously or initialed at first and afterward with Blair's name, and edited with a memoir by William Mason in the mid-century editions, which fixed the text and the biography. The years of composition are uncertain and are not asserted.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1743; the earliest editions carried no full author's name, and the poem was repeatedly reissued, enlarged and illustrated, including in editions with designs after William Hogarth and with William Mason's 'Memoir of the Author'. Blair's own text and the sequence of his shorter poems were settled by modern scholarly edition.

title: The Tomb
description: Robert Blair's projected companion to 'The Grave', left in manuscript at his death and printed among his posthumous poems. It pursues the same subject in the same measure, but narrows the focus to the sepulchre itself and to the monuments and inscriptions by which the living attempt to keep the dead in mind.
plot_or_argument: Like 'The Grave', the poem is an exercise of thought rather than a narrative. It meditates upon the tomb as a structure, an inscription and a hope: the masonry and the heraldry of memorial are surveyed and found insufficient, while the Christian tomb is read as the pledge of a resurrection. The turn from the vanity of monumental fame to the faith of the buried believer is the argument, and the piece supplies a closing reflection to the open-ended contemplation of its predecessor.
narrative_structure: A continuous meditation addressed to the tomb, in the same sectional, associative movement as 'The Grave', with apostrophe and epitaph-like reflection taking the place of events.
literary_form: Meditative blank-verse poem, a planned sequel or pendant to 'The Grave', surviving among the manuscripts Blair left and printed posthumously; short in relation to its companion and incomplete in the sense that its author left it.
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter in the same weighty, Latinate manner as 'The Grave'; the diction is funerary and lapidary, with the compressed phrasing of an epitaph.
historical_context: It was written in the same period as 'The Grave', when Blair was assembling a sequence of poems on the last things, and it stands within the 1740s fashion for churchyard, tomb and resurrection meditation. Its survival in manuscript and its posthumous printing are part of the history of that fashion, since the editors of Blair's papers were also the editors of his reputation.
literary_significance: It completes the conception of 'The Grave' and shows how far the graveyard meditation had become, in Blair's hands, a structured sequence rather than a single performance. It is a minor but authentic document of the preromantic contemplation of death.
attribution_notes: Attribution to Blair is not contested; the difficulty lies in its publication history. Because it was not printed in the poet's lifetime and because the several posthumous collections and reissues of Blair's poems are differently dated, no first-print year is asserted here and the publication field is left null rather than guessed.
bibliographical_notes: Left in manuscript at Blair's death in 1746 and issued among the posthumous poems printed in London and Edinburgh during the following decades, in editions associated with William Mason's memoir and with the later collected texts. Any specific first-publication year given in the secondary literature is disputed in detail and is therefore not recorded here.

title: The Ruins of Rome
description: John Dyer's first poem and one of the most remarkable of Augustan ruin meditations: a topographical and philosophical survey of the fallen city of Rome, written by an English country curate who had made the Grand Tour. It was printed anonymously, and its attribution to Dyer rests on contemporary notice and on the later collection of his verse. The manner is deliberately archaising and sonorous, closer to a Latin or Italian 'grand manner' than to the couplet idioms of his English contemporaries.
plot_or_argument: The poem is a description which becomes a philosophy of history. The traveller moves over the ruins, the aqueducts, the broken statues and the buried bases of the city, and from their mass and fragments draws an argument about the transience of empire and the mortality of glory. Rome is at once a moral spectacle and a Christian one: the pagan capital that conquered the world has been conquered by time, and the modern papal city that sits among the ruins supplies a second lesson on the revolutions of power and on the providential government of nations. The moral energy of the piece is spent on the disproportion between the grandeur of what was and the meanness of what remains.
narrative_structure: A continuous descriptivo-philosophical poem following the topography of the ruins, with the traveller's present survey, the recollected history of the republic and empire, and the Christian and modern city interwoven without formal division.
principal_characters: The surveying traveller-poet; personified Rome and her ruins
literary_form: Topographical and meditative poem in the manner of the 'ruins' tradition, combining description, historical narration and reflection; a single sustained line of verse addressed to no auditor.
meter_and_prosody: Predominantly decasyllabic English heroic measure handled with marked asperity: long Latinate compounds, hypermetric and stretched lines, and a deliberate refusal of couplet neatness, giving the blank-verse-like solemnity Dyer thought proper to his subject.
historical_context: It appears in the aftermath of the second decade of Grand Tour travel and of the growing English quarrel about taste, precedent and Gothic versus classical authority, and it takes the ruins of Rome as the emblem of national and imperial decline at a moment when British commerce and empire were beginning to make that emblem urgent. Its classical-subject treatment in unpolished native verse was itself a position in the debate about the reach of English poetry.
literary_significance: It is the earliest and one of the strangest of the eighteenth-century English poems about imperial decay, and it established the harsh, 'sublime and antique' voice that Johnson, in his life of Dyer, described as a deliberate attempt to naturalise Latin majesty in English measure. It stands between Thomson's meditative topography and the ruin-poetry of the following century, and it is a source text for the age's association of topography with the philosophy of history.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously in 1740; the ascription to Dyer rests on contemporary attribution and on the inclusion of the poem in collections of his work, and it is now universally accepted. Because the first edition was unsigned, the record is entered under 'attributed'.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1740 as 'The Ruins of Rome. A Poem', anonymous; reprinted among Dyer's poems in the collected editions of the later eighteenth century. Composition is generally placed in the years immediately following the author's Italian travel; no specific year is asserted.

title: The Fleece
description: John Dyer's principal poem: a didactic and topographical work on the English wool trade, from the feeding of the sheep and the shearing to the staple, the marketing and the international commerce that carried the fleece to the world's ends. It was published by subscription and carries the name of the clergyman who wrote it. The ambition is at once technical and moral: to make the whole circuit of a national industry the subject of elevated unrhymed verse.
plot_or_argument: The poem moves outward in stages from the pasture to the ocean. Its first care is practical: the breeds, the feeding, the shearing and the management of the flock, with the shepherd and the shepherdess introduced as figures of a vanishing rural order. From the fleece in the fold it passes to the wool in the warehouse and the market, and then to the merchant, the ship and the ports of the Mediterranean and the north, arguing that this single commodity has bound England into the world's trade. A moral anxiety runs under the praise: the growth of wealth threatens to corrupt the labour and the independence that produced it, and the prospect of national fullness is shadowed by the fear of decline. The argument is therefore a sustained piece of political economy in verse, closer to a discourse of the wool trade than to any earlier English poem.
narrative_structure: A didactic poem in books, each gathering its own department of the subject, with descriptive digression, apostrophe to the labouring poor, and an ascending sweep from local husbandry to global commerce.
principal_characters: The shepherd and shepherdess of the English hills; the wool merchant; the mariner; the labouring poor of the staple towns
literary_form: Didactic and topographical poem in the Thomson school, in books, with the technical instruction of a husbandry poem combined with the survey of a trade; issued after subscription proposals and dedications.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter) of notoriously harsh and laborious texture, with long compounds, stretched and hypermetric lines, and an evident attempt to bend English measure to the weight of Latin and Italian syntax.
historical_context: It was written in the decades when the wool and cloth trade was the acknowledged foundation of English national power, and when the staple, the export markets and the growing manufactures were matters of public debate. Dyer, a Welsh-born curate with a small living and large schemes for rural industry, published by subscription after earlier ventures failed, and the poem carries those projects' hopes and disappointments.
literary_significance: It is the most ambitious of the eighteenth-century attempts to put a national industry into elevated verse, and the crucial link between Thomson's meditative topography and Goldsmith's 'The Deserted Village' in the poetry of rural labour, commerce and depopulation. Samuel Johnson's account of its crabbed sublimity made it the standard example of a poet who mistook harshness for strength, and it remains a primary document of the age's thinking about commerce and its discontents.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was published in the author's own name in the collected editions and its composition is documented in Dyer's correspondence with his friends. Precise years of composition for the individual books are not fixed here and are left null.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1757, in books, by subscription; reprinted among the collected poems of Dyer published soon after his death and in later editions. No printer is asserted beyond the 1757 imprint.

title: The Tournament
description: One of the longest and most ambitious of the poems Thomas Chatterton put into the name of the fifteenth-century Bristol monk Thomas Rowley, and a centrepiece of the forgeries he sent to Horace Walpole in 1764. It presents itself as an antiquarian account of a medieval tournament, complete with lists of champions, devices and heraldic blazon, in a deliberately archaized spelling and diction. Its interest is double: as an early achievement of the primitive-genius vogue, and as a document of a Bristol apprentice's furious self-education in the literature of the past.
plot_or_argument: The poem narrates the summoning, the gathering and the running of a great tournament, and dwells on the heraldry, the armour, the ladies' favours and the encounters of the champions with a minuteness meant to look like a period chronicler's rather than a modern poet's imagination. Chivalric honour, religious invocation and the pomp of the field are combined without any neoclassical sense of proportion, so that the piece reads as a series of illuminated tableaux. Its frame is the more important fiction: Rowley is made to be an eyewitness and recorder of the scene, an authority older than any modern antiquary. The result is the most complete of Chatterton's impersonations, in which the medieval is not described from outside but re-enacted in a language the eighteenth century was willing to believe.
narrative_structure: A chronicle-poem in the supposed voice and hand of Rowley: annalistic opening, catalogue of champions and devices, narrative of the field, and devotional and heraldic digression, without regular stanzaic closure.
principal_characters: The framing chronicler 'Thomas Rowley'; the knights and champions of the listed tournament; the ladies whose favours are proclaimed
literary_form: Antiquarian romance in verse among the Rowley poems; long, irregular and catalogue-driven, in the archaic orthography Chatterton supplied, with glosses of the obsolete words attached in the manuscripts and collections.
meter_and_prosody: Rowley's supposed measures: long lines with medial caesura and mixed rhyme formations, imitating fifteenth-century verse rather than any Elizabethan or Augustan practice.
historical_context: It belongs to the Rowley correspondence of 1764, when Chatterton, a clerk in Bristol, supplied Walpole with parchment 'originals' and letters in a fabricated antiquarian persona, at the moment when the taste for chivalry and for national origins was being formed by Walpole's own circle at Strawberry Hill. The forgery was detected within a few years, but the poems continued to be read as poetry.
literary_significance: It is the largest single exercise in the Rowley impersonation and an important text in the history of literary forgery, of medievalism, and of the cult of the primitive genius; its mixture of heraldic learning and genuine imaginative power is what later readers from the Romantics onwards remembered. It also helped to establish the vogue for an invented national antiquity which the same decade received from Macpherson and from Percy.
attribution_notes: Authorship is recorded as single because Chatterton, not any medieval monk, wrote the poem. The ascription in the manuscripts is to 'Thomas Rowley', a fictitious fifteenth-century Bristol priest and chronicler whose parchment 'originals' and glosses Chatterton supplied; the deception imposed upon Walpole and other antiquaries before it was seen through. The year 1764 refers to the Rowley correspondence in which the piece was produced.
bibliographical_notes: Not printed in Chatterton's lifetime in a form datable with confidence here; it passed with the other Rowley pieces into the periodical press and into the collected editions of Chatterton's works issued after his death in 1770, so the publication year is left null. The bundle sent to Walpole in 1764 is the documentary anchor for its composition.

title: The Battle of Hastings
alternative_titles: A Battle of Hastings (ascribed to Rowley)
description: The most considerable of the narrative poems Chatterton attributed to Thomas Rowley: a 'Saxon' account of the Norman conquest of England, planned on an epic scale and written in a heroic measure that Chatterton supposed to be the practice of the fifteenth century. It is at once a battle poem, a patriotic history of the defeated English, and a further stage in the Rowley forgeries.
plot_or_argument: The subject is the crisis of the year 1066 and the subjection of the English to a foreign conqueror, treated with the sympathies firmly on the side of the losing nation. The poem opens by invoking the patron and the muse of the intended work, gathers the Saxon host and its leaders, and passes to the shock of the field and to the lament over what England lost. Chatterton's interest is in the dignity and the misery of a conquered people rather than in a regular epic machinery, and the piece survives as the projected opening of a design that was never finished. Its argument is thus double: a narrative of defeat, and an imitation of an 'ancient' national epic believed capable of arousing patriotic feeling.
narrative_structure: An unfinished epic design: invocation and proposition, mustering and battle, lament and prophetic retrospect on English liberty under the conqueror, in the annalistic manner Chatterton assigned to Rowley.
principal_characters: The Saxon leaders and their host; the Norman conqueror; the conquered English people; the framing chronicler 'Thomas Rowley'
literary_form: Projected national epic in the Rowley manner, with antiquarian gloss and an analysis of the intended work attached; heroic-length lines rather than the couplet of contemporary epic practice.
meter_and_prosody: Long decasyllabic and eleven-syllable heroic measure in Chatterton's archaising imitation of early English verse, with heavy sounding of old names and a deliberate roughness contemporaries accepted as antique evidence.
historical_context: It stands within the Rowley papers of Chatterton's last Bristol years, and within the wider 1760s revival of the Saxon and 'Gothic' past as a source of native liberty and of poetic sublimity. The conquest theme was a live political myth in Augustan England, and Chatterton turns a schoolroom subject into an imagined national epic.
literary_significance: It is the strongest evidence that the Rowley forgeries were not merely antiquarian hoaxes but an attempt to reconstruct an English epic tradition older than the Norman conquest, and it influenced the later vogue for Saxon and British subjects in poetry and in the novel. It also stands as one of the founding documents of English medievalism and of the romantic cult of unfinished genius.
attribution_notes: Written by Chatterton and ascribed in the manuscripts and collections to the fictitious Thomas Rowley; no medieval original exists, and the 'ancient' authorship was a forgery discredited by the antiquarian inquiry into the Rowley papers. Composition and first-print dates are left null because the chronology of the surviving papers is debated.
bibliographical_notes: Transmitted among the Rowley manuscripts and printed after Chatterton's death in the successive collections of his poems and in the periodical press that carried the Rowley series. No first-print year is asserted here.

title: The Pilgrimage
description: A shorter poem of the Rowley series, in which Chatterton depicts a company of pilgrims making their way to a holy shrine. It belongs to the devotional and descriptive side of the forgeries, and shows Chatterton using the supposed licence of an earlier and simpler age to write religious poetry that no Augustan poet publishing under his own name could have offered.
plot_or_argument: The piece describes the progress of the pilgrimage and the scenes and people it passes: the shrine and its offerings, the devotion of the company, and the rough, homely and unsolemn life of the road. The emphasis falls on the externals of an older popular religion, treated with affection and with a frankness Chatterton thought characteristic of a time before politeness had refined devotion into decorum. There is no dramatic conflict; the interest is pictorial and vocal, sustained by the archaized diction which carries the fiction of date. The underlying argument is that a nation's religion, like its poetry, is most powerful when it is most naive.
narrative_structure: A processional poem: the pilgrimage observed in a sequence of descriptive and apostrophic passages, with invocation and devotional address framing the movement.
principal_characters: The pilgrim company; the shrine and its keepers; the framing poet 'Thomas Rowley'
literary_form: Devotional-descriptive poem in the Rowley manner, with obsolete diction and gloss; closer to a popular song or carol tradition than to the chronicle-poems of the same series.
meter_and_prosody: Rowley's irregular long measure, with a strong lyric and song-like beat in parts, in deliberately antique spelling; the harshness of the sound is part of the designed effect.
historical_context: It is one of the pieces that went out under Rowley's name in the Bristol correspondence of the mid 1760s, at a time when the collecting of old English poetry was becoming a fashionable antiquarian pursuit and when pilgrimage, shrines and popular superstition were being reinterpreted as picturesque national material.
literary_significance: It is a striking example of the religious imagination available within the forgery: Chatterton invented not only an antique manner but an entire devotional culture, and the poem helped to form the later romantic and antiquarian interest in medieval popular piety. Its frankness about the bodily and homely side of devotion anticipates the romantic recovery of the Middle Ages.
attribution_notes: Authored by Chatterton though ascribed in the Rowley papers to the fictitious monk; no medieval original exists, and the 'antiquity' of the piece rests on forged manuscripts and glosses. Its place in the series and its date of composition are not fixed with confidence, so the year fields are left null.
bibliographical_notes: Preserved among the Rowley papers and printed after Chatterton's death in the collected editions of his poems and in the periodical press that carried the Rowley series; the first-print year is not asserted here.

title: The Balade of Charitie
alternative_titles: A Ballad of Charitie (ascribed to Rowley)
description: The best-known of Chatterton's short Rowley poems: a religious ballad in praise of Christian charity, put out as the work of the fifteenth-century Bristol monk and dated by its ascription to an earlier century still. It is at once an exemplum of alms-deeds and a piece of invented antiquity, and it has had a longer independent life in anthologies than almost any other of the Rowley poems.
plot_or_argument: The ballad's argument is an encomium of the virtue of charity and a warning against the neglect of it. It opens by invoking charity as a heavenly quality with authority over earthly judgement, and then illustrates its thesis with the fate of a shelterless wanderer turned from the doors she begs at and left unrelieved, so that religious instruction becomes social accusation. The closing movement turns the dead wanderer into a judgement on the uncharitable, and sets the virtue of pity against the pomp of rites and of endowed devotion. It is therefore a poem about the obligations of wealth to visible poverty, framed as an old popular ballad.
narrative_structure: A short exemplum-ballad: invocation and doctrinal statement, the narrative instance of the rejected wanderer, and a moral-judgement conclusion, in the order of a preacher's example rather than of a plot.
principal_characters: Charity personified as the invoked virtue; the unsheltered wanderer; the householders who turn her from their doors
literary_form: Ballad in the antique manner with an exemplum structure, printed among the Rowley poems with obsolete spelling and gloss; one of the pieces Chatterton supplied to the fashionable taste for old popular poetry.
meter_and_prosody: Stanzaic ballad measure in Chatterton's archaising imitation, with echoing rhyme and a weight of obsolete diction; the deliberate uncouthness of sound is the poem's evidence of age.
historical_context: It belongs to the Rowley papers and to the mid-1760s rush of enthusiasm for old English poetry, when Walpole, Percy and their readers were collecting and reprinting ballads and when the charity sermon in verse was a living form. Its subject of neglected poverty had immediate force in a culture beginning to debate poor laws, alms and the duties of the rich.
literary_significance: It gave the Rowley forgeries their most durable lyric, and its standing with later poets is remarkable: Wordsworth defended and quoted it in 'The Prelude' as a specimen of genuine national poetry, which shows how completely the fiction of antiquity could survive the exposure of the fraud. It is a key text for the afterlife of literary forgery in romantic taste.
attribution_notes: Written by Chatterton and ascribed to Thomas Rowley, with a fabricated earlier date attached in the manuscripts; the 'antient' authorship is a forgery and is recorded as such, while the poem's own authorship is undisputed. Composition and first-print years are left null because the dating within the Rowley papers is not settled.
bibliographical_notes: Transmitted among the Rowley papers and printed in the posthumous collections of Chatterton's poems; it entered the standard anthologies of English lyric and was quoted by Wordsworth in the later books of 'The Prelude'. No first-print year is asserted here.

title: Fragments of Ancient Poetry, Collected from the Bards
description: James Macpherson's first Ossianic publication: a thin collection of short pieces offered as translations from the Gaelic or Erse of 'ancient bards', with the names of the heroic cycle attached to them. It appeared anonymously, with a list of subscribers prefixed, and its success sent its author into the Highlands to collect more. It is the opening document of one of the great literary controversies of the century.
plot_or_argument: There is no sustained argument, only a series of brief lyrical and narrative fragments: invocations of heroes, laments for the dead, addresses to the night, to mountains and to departed glory. The pieces are unified by a tone of mournful sublimity and by a supposed antiquity, since the speaker throughout is a bard of an unrecorded heroic age reporting what older bards sang. The effect the collection aims at is the impression of a native epic tradition surviving in ruins, and its politics of the fragment is deliberate: what is missing is made to appear lost rather than never written. The book's dedication and advertisements frame the fragments as a national restoration of ancient Scottish poetry, and they promised further and larger recoveries.
narrative_structure: A collection of independent short pieces, sequenced for variety of tone rather than chronology, prefaced by subscriber list and advertisements and annotated with the names of the heroes and the occasions of the songs.
principal_characters: The supposed ancient bards; the heroes and heroines of the Gaelic cycle invoked in the fragments
literary_form: Anthology of translated fragments in prose-verse arrangement, with prefatory and paratextual matter asserting their antiquity and their source language; the unit is the short lyric or the broken narrative.
meter_and_prosody: A stern, inverted, cadenced English prose-verse of long periods and heavy latinate diction, modelled on no existing English measure; the irregular 'ancient' rhythm was one of the features that readers seized on as evidence of sublimity and sceptics seized on as evidence of imposition.
historical_context: It was published in Edinburgh in 1760, in the moment after the 'Forty-five' when Scottish Highland antiquity was being simultaneously romanticised and policed, and within the wider European argument about primitive genius, Homer and the origins of national poetry that had been sharpened by Hurd, Blair and the Warton circle. Hugh Blair's encouragement and the subscription model made the first collection possible.
literary_significance: It started the Ossian phenomenon and with it the European fashion for the primitive sublime, the forged or reconstructed national epic, and the cult of the bard. Its manner is traceable through the following decade's poetry, and its controversy set the terms in which authentication, national literary property and editorial honesty were debated.
attribution_notes: Macpherson is the author in the sense that he produced and published the texts; whether he translated genuine Gaelic and Irish sources or largely composed his 'ancients' himself has been disputed from 1760 to the present, and the 'ancient bard' authorship the title asserts is certainly not verifiable. The present record assigns the book to Macpherson and marks the ancient attribution as disputed.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in Edinburgh in 1760, anonymously, with a list of subscribers prefixed; later reprinted within the collected Ossianic editions. The Gaelic sources Macpherson claimed to have transcribed have not been traced to manuscripts of the required date, which is the ground of the enduring dispute.

title: Fingal
description: Macpherson's first long Ossianic poem, offered as an ancient epic in six books on the deeds of Fingal, the Caledonian hero, together with several shorter translated poems. It greatly enlarges the manner of the 'Fragments' into a narrative machine of invasions, single combats, ghosts and bardic recitation. Its publication, with a prefacial dissertation, provoked both enthusiasm in Europe and attack at home.
plot_or_argument: The epic frame is a war in which the forces of the north and of Ireland contend, and Fingal, aged, venerable and supreme in judgement as well as in arms, leads his Caledonians to the relief of the distressed. The action is interrupted and deepened by the recursive method of the poems: bards sing the past, heroes recount their own sorrows, and the ghosts of the departed appear to hasten or to lament a death. Love, friendship and the observance of hospitality are the governing virtues, and the great motive power is grief, expressed in lamentation over the slain and over fallen greatness. The shorter poems appended are mostly laments and narratives of private calamity, and they supply the tenderness the epic's battles refuse.
narrative_structure: An epic in six books with a strongly episodic and recursive organisation: the present action is repeatedly suspended by songs, recitations and visions of the past, so that the temporal structure is that of an ancient tradition recollected by bards rather than of a continuous plot.
principal_characters: Fingal; his sons and warriors; the heroes and heroines of the appended poems; the spirits of the dead and the reciting bards
literary_form: Ancient epic in the restored or reconstructed manner, in books, with argument or analysis prefixed to each book and with introductory and explanatory dissertation; accompanied by a group of shorter songs and laments.
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed cadenced verse of great uniformity and weight, with inversion, accumulation of epithets, and long rolling periods; the measure is deliberately unlike heroick couplet or blank verse of the Augustan school, and was admired as a recovery of ancient harmonious barbaric numbers.
historical_context: Published in 1762, in the war years, when Scottish and English readers were being offered national epics on every side, and when the dissertation on ancient poetry prefixed to the work was itself a contribution to the criticism of taste and sublimity. The volume's success established Macpherson's position and his claim to have recovered a Homeric-age literature from the Gaelic.
literary_significance: It is the founding text of the Ossianic vogue in its full epic form, and one of the most widely translated and imitated poems of the later eighteenth century in Europe; its machinery of grief, mist, ghosts and heroic moderation supplied preromantic poetry with a whole repertoire. Its claim to have supplied Britain with an ancient epic of its own remains the centre of the authentication controversy.
attribution_notes: Recorded as disputed because Macpherson published the work as a translation of an ancient epic and contemporaries, and many since, have held that the ancient original is largely or wholly his own composition, made from such Gaelic tradition as he genuinely gathered. The ascription to 'Ossian' and to the ancient bards is not verifiable; Macpherson's own responsibility for the printed text is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1762 as 'Fingal, an ancient Epic Poem', in six books, together with several other poems, with prefatory dissertation; reprinted within 'The Works of Ossian' and in many later editions, British and foreign. No printer is asserted here beyond the year and the fact of the accompanying apparatus.

title: Temora
description: Macpherson's second and longer Ossianic epic, offered as a translation of ancient poems on the war for the Irish throne and on the hill and hall of Temora. It carries a more elaborate scholarly apparatus than 'Fingal', including an introductory dissertation and translations of shorter Irish remains, and it presses further after a regular heroic structure.
plot_or_argument: The action concerns the invasion of Ireland and the contest between an expelled family and an usurping line, with Fingal again the arbiter of the north whose arms decide the quarrel. The poem's real subject, as its contemporaries saw, is the moral cost of war: its chiefs are magnanimous, wounded and funereal, and its interest is concentrated on combats, deaths and laments rather than on the mechanics of plot. Love and friendship run through the action in the persons of the young heroes and their mistresses, and the machinery is provided by the spirits and the reciting bards of the earlier poem. The design is closer to the classical epic than 'Fingal', and its ambition is explicitly to restore the 'epopoeia' of the ancient northern nations.
narrative_structure: An epic in books with a continuous central action, framed by an introductory dissertation, and reinforced by the shorter poems and the prose fragments appended; internal recitation and prophecy still interrupt the sequence.
principal_characters: Fingal and his sons; the competing Irish chiefs of the war for Temora; the young lovers of the episode; the spirits and bards
literary_form: Restored ancient epic in books, with argument, dissertation and explanatory notes, and with an apparatus of translated Irish and Highland remains attached to support the claim of source.
meter_and_prosody: The ossianic cadence continued: unrhymed, heavily accented and inverted periods of long decasyllabic and alexandrine-like measure, with sustained apostrophe and epithet; the rhythm is the poem's principal claim to authenticity and to sublimity.
historical_context: It followed 'Fingal' within a year, at the high point of Macpherson's credit, and appeared amid a swelling controversy over the manuscripts, in which Highland gentlemen and Irish scholars were invited to verify what he had transcribed. Its Irish setting drew upon the antiquarian knowledge of the Gaelic nations then being assembled by writers such as Charles O'Conor, whose attacks on the forgeries came soon after.
literary_significance: It completed the Ossianic corpus as an epic system and fixed the European image of the ancient northern world as a scene of gloomy sublimity, generous enmity and funerary tenderness. Its reception, from German poets and painters to English reviewers, is one of the largest episodes in the history of literary forgery and of the primitive-genius doctrine.
attribution_notes: As with the other Ossianic publications the ancient authorship is disputed: Macpherson offered the work as a translation from Gaelic originals of the heroic era, and the charge that he composed them, on slight foundation, has never been fully withdrawn. The record assigns the printed text to Macpherson and marks the claimed ancient source as contested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1763 as 'Temora, an ancient Epic Poem', with an introduction and dissertation; consolidated with 'Fingal' in the collected edition of 1765 and in the later editions, including the posthumous reprints with which the Gaelic source question continued to be argued.

title: The Works of Ossian
description: The collected edition in which Macpherson gathered the fragments and the two epics, with a large scholarly apparatus of dissertations, imitations of ancient poems and a history of the era, and which gave Europe 'Ossian' as a single book. This is the form in which the poems were read, translated, attacked and imitated for the rest of the century, and the volume round which the authentication quarrel hardened.
plot_or_argument: As a collected work it presents a complete imagined literature: the epic actions of Fingal and of his grandson, the shorter poems of lament and of love, and the critical dissertations that supply a chronology, a bardic religion and a theory of ancient heroic poetry. Its argument throughout is that the northern nations possessed, before letters, a poetry of passion and of the moral imagination equal to the classical epic, and that this poetry can be recovered by a modern translator. The shorter pieces add the tender and domestic register: the dead mourned by women, the ghosts of the fallen, the last departures of a failing race. The volume closes the circle by making the reader's own sensibility the proof of the poems' truth.
narrative_structure: A collected two-volume edition: preliminary dissertations on the era and on the heroic poetry of the ancients, the epics, the shorter poems and translations, with arguments and notes; the sequence is encyclopaedic rather than narrative.
principal_characters: Ossian as the supposed ancient author and speaker; Fingal; his sons and successors; the bards, spirits and mourning women of the shorter poems
literary_form: Collected translated epic and lyric corpus with editorial dissertation and annotation: the founding edition of the Ossianic canon, and the vehicle for its scholarly defence.
meter_and_prosody: The uniform cadenced unrhymed measure of the Ossianic books, with the shorter poems in a more purely lyric and elegiacal movement; apostrophe, epithet and inverted syntax carry the rhythm.
historical_context: Published in 1765, after the controversy had already become public and political, and at the moment when the Highland Society, Irish antiquaries and English critics were all examining the claims. The edition's apparatus is an answer to that scrutiny, and its confidence provoked the more systematic denials of the later eighteenth century.
literary_significance: It is one of the most influential books of the second half of the century across Europe, the standard reference for the primitive sublime, for the poetry of melancholy and for the idea of a national bardic literature; its influence is traceable in poetry, in the Gothic, in music and in painting. It is also the most celebrated case in the history of literary forgery or reconstruction, and it forced the age to define the evidence required for a text's antiquity.
attribution_notes: The collection is Macpherson's in every recoverable sense, and the ancient authorship it asserts, that of the bard Ossian, is recorded here as disputed: the claimed Gaelic and Irish originals have never been authenticated, and the case for composition rather than translation was made within a few years of publication and renewed since. The edition's own dissertations are Macpherson's defence.
bibliographical_notes: First collected edition printed in London in 1765 in two volumes, with the preliminary dissertations and notes; reprinted throughout the century in British, Irish and continental editions, some of them with the disputed Gaelic texts appended. No printer is asserted beyond the imprint year.

title: Reliques of Ancient English Poetry
description: Thomas Percy's three-volume collection of early English ballads, songs and other poetical remains, with prefatory essays, historical and critical notes and a life of several of the old poets: the book that made the native ballad tradition available to the polite reader and turned it into a subject of criticism. It drew on a recovered manuscript folio of ballads and on printed copies, and it presented the material in a carefully arranged historical order. Its editorial practice, modernising and repairing the old texts, was at once its popular strength and the ground of the quarrel about it.
plot_or_argument: As a collection its argument is a history of English poetry told in specimens: that the native tradition, from the minstrelsy of the north through the ballad and the romance, possessed a genuine pathos, harmony and strength of description which the later 'polite' age undervalued. The volumes interleave heroic songs, ballads of love and chivalry, fragments of old romance, and pieces of lyric and devotional poetry, with critical remarks on each and with the famous defence of the 'antient' poets in the prefacial essay on minstrelsy. Percy also let the reader see the editorial hand: texts were amended, completed from other copies, and in places composed or interpolated where the original was judged defective, in the belief that he was restoring an ancient author's meaning. The collection thus argues two things at once, that English poetry has an ancient native inheritance, and that a modern editor of taste is its rightful guardian.
narrative_structure: A chronological and thematic anthology in three volumes, each book of specimens preceded or followed by historical and critical observation, with a preliminary essay and with notes, glossaries and life accounts attached to individual pieces.
principal_characters: The anonymous and named old poets and 'minstrels' whose songs are collected; the editors and printers whose copies are collated; Percy himself as the arranging and annotating voice
literary_form: Anthology of editorial collection: ballads, songs, romances and fragments, printed with preface, essays, arguments, annotations and glossary; the founding model of the scholarly-popular national anthology.
meter_and_prosody: The whole range of early English verse as Percy understood it: ballad stanzas of common and of long measure, the stanzaic forms of the native romance, and the several kinds of old English verse he set out to distinguish; the printed texts are smoothed toward modern regularity.
historical_context: It appears at the centre of the 1760s revival of interest in national antiquity, alongside Chatterton's Rowley forgeries, Macpherson's Ossian and the debates over primitive genius, and it was edited by a clergyman-antiquary with patrons in the great houses, later himself a bishop in Ireland. Its appearance also coincides with the quarrel over editorial fidelity, in which Percy was attacked for modernising and for pretending to restore what he had in fact rewritten.
literary_significance: It is the single most influential book of old English poetry of the century: it formed the taste of the Romantic poets for the ballad, revived the native tradition as a source of poetical pleasure, and established the anthology-with-notes as a critical genre. Both its method and its materials were answered and extended by later collectors, and its influence on the ballad revivals of the 1780s and 1790s is direct.
attribution_notes: Percy is the editor and the responsibility for the arrangement, essays and the amended texts is his; the individual poems are of course anonymous and attributed within the volumes with varying degrees of confidence. Some pieces were printed from the folio manuscript he recovered, others from broadsides and earlier copies, and a number were repaired or completed by the editor, which is the notorious part of the book's attribution history.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1765 in three volumes, with a dedication to the Earl of Huntingdon, and enlarged and revised in several subsequent editions during Percy's lifetime; the manuscript basis includes the folio of old ballads Percy acquired from a printing house, since known as the Percy Folio.

title: Hungarian Traductions
alternative_titles: Hungarian Traductions, from the Best Latin and Other Historians
original_language: English (translated from Latin and other languages)
description: Percy's earliest book-length publication as a translator and compiler: a volume of renderings from the Latin and other historians of Hungary, offering the English reader an account of the Hungarians and of the long frontier warfare of eastern Europe with the Ottoman powers. It is a work of the same antiquarian-historical imagination that produced the 'Reliques', applied to the origins and fortunes of a nation rather than to its poetry.
plot_or_argument: The volume has no plot but an assembling argument: that the history of Hungary, its people, their migrations, their institutions and their struggles, can be recovered for English readers from the foreign historians and made intelligible as a single narrative of national fortune. Its substance is the rise and the trials of a nation placed on the border of empires, with the incursions of eastern peoples, the contests with the Turks, and the revolutions of its own dynasties treated as a lesson in the mutability of states. Percy's editorial interest shows itself in the choice and arrangement of the pieces and in the notes, which pursue the origin, manners and antiquities of the nations described. The implicit argument is that national character, like national poetry, is a proper object of study and of sympathetic curiosity.
narrative_structure: A compiled and translated historical miscellany: independent rendered pieces and extracts arranged to give a continuous account of the nation and its wars, with editorial notes and prefatory matter.
principal_characters: The Hungarian nation as collective subject; the kings and commanders of the translated histories; the Ottoman and neighbouring powers
literary_form: Translation and editorial compilation in prose, of historical and antiquarian material, with notes and prefatory argument; a work of national history in the translated-compiler manner of the period.
historical_context: It was published a year before the 'Reliques', when Percy was establishing himself as a compiler-antiquary supported by noble patronage, and when the history and present condition of the eastern European frontier was of live interest to a British reading public following Habsburg and Ottoman affairs. It belongs to the same antiquarian temper as his ballad collection, an interest in the origins and character of nations.
literary_significance: It is the lesser-known but revealing foundation of Percy's career, showing that the editor of the 'Reliques' began as a translator of national history, and that his project throughout was the recovery of the particular character of nations. It is a useful document of the eighteenth-century habit of making other countries' histories available through compiled translation.
attribution_notes: Attribution to Percy as translator and compiler is uncontested; the underlying historians are of course several and are named in the volume. The dates of the original pieces and of Percy's work upon them are not fixed here, so the composition fields are left null.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1764; it was privately circulated in a small run and its sheets were subsequently drawn on by Percy for antiquarian and historical matter, a fact often noticed in accounts of his early publications. No printer is asserted beyond the 1764 imprint.

title: Five Varieties of Blank Verse
alternative_titles: Five Varieties of Blank Verse, which are found to have been practised by some of our best English Poets
description: A short metrical treatise by Percy, issued as a companion to the historical criticism of the 'Reliques', which distinguishes five varieties of unrhymed English verse and traces them from the age of Gower to that of Milton. It is one of the earliest attempts in English to describe the history of blank verse as a system of measurable forms rather than as a single practice, and it belongs to the editorial apparatus of the antiquarian revival of native poetry.
plot_or_argument: The treatise argues that English unrhymed verse is not one measure but several, and it sets out the varieties with specimens of each, arranged in chronological order so that the reader may see the progress of the metre towards the established iambic pentameter of the later poets. The point is both technical and national: the Old English and early writers had a metrical art of their own, and the modern habit of reading them as irregular or barbarous arises from ignorance of the distinction. Percy's evidence is scanned quotation, and his method is that of the antiquary-critic who lets specimens carry the argument. The essay thus supports the larger case of the 'Reliques', that native antiquity deserves critical as well as historical attention.
narrative_structure: A continuous argument in a single short tract: proposition, definition and naming of each variety, illustrative specimens in sequence, and concluding remarks on the ascent of the measure to Milton.
literary_form: Critical treatise in versification, printed as a separate tract and reissued among the apparatus of the collected editions of old English poetry; its method is definitional and illustrative, with quoted specimens.
meter_and_prosody: Prose argument on verse: the subject-matter is the analysis of English accentual and syllabic measures, including the long unrhymed line, the twelve-syllable line of the Romance school, and the several varieties of the decasyllable, with scanning of each.
historical_context: It appears with the first vogue of the 'Reliques' and in the middle of the 1760s debate about old English verse, blank verse and the rules, in which the antiquaries were revising the neoclassical account of the metrical history of the language. It is a scholarly by-product of the ballad collection's enterprise.
literary_significance: It is a foundation-stone of the history of English metrics, the first systematic attempt to classify the varieties of unrhymed native verse, and it prepared the way for the later scholarship of the early English measures and for the antiquarian defence of blank verse as a national form.
attribution_notes: Attribution to Percy is regular and undisputed. Its precise first-print circumstances and its relation to the several editions of the 'Reliques' are complicated, and the composition dates are not fixed; the year recorded is that of its publication as a separate metrical tract of the same moment as the collection.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in 1765 as a short tract and subsequently reprinted within the enlarged editions of the 'Reliques' as part of their critical apparatus; the copies consulted for this record are the collected reissues rather than a separately identified first print, whose details are not asserted here.

title: An Enquiry into the Present State of Polite Learning in Europe
alternative_titles: Enquiry into the Present State of Polite Learning
description: Oliver Goldsmith's first important prose work, and one of the most quoted books of the age about the condition of letters: an enquiry into the state of polite learning in the nations of Europe, written by a man about to try his fortune in London. It is at once a comparative survey of national cultures, a history of the progress of the arts, and a bitter account of the decay of patronage and of the degraded condition of the modern writer.
plot_or_argument: The enquiry proceeds from the general to the national and from the historical to the immediately contemporary. Goldsmith argues that the polite arts have in general advanced, that ignorance and superstition have been expelled by the spread of learning, and that the modern nations of Europe, France, Italy, Spain, Germany, Poland and the northern kingdoms, each display their own mixture of cultivation and remaining barbarism. Turning to England, he complains that while every other branch of knowledge has improved, literature alone has declined, and he assigns the decline to identifiable causes: the withdrawal of noble and royal patronage, the pride and avarice of the great who would direct as well as reward, the multiplication of critics and reviewers, the corruption of the theatre, and the deplorable economics of the book trade, which leaves the man of letters dependent upon his humour and his creditors. The book's most durable passages are those in which the writer's poverty, his patience and his independence are analysed as a social condition rather than as private misfortune.
narrative_structure: A sustained argumentative enquiry in twenty sections, proceeding historically and comparatively, with each nation and each branch of the polite arts taken in turn and with the English case reserved for the closing and most personal complaints.
principal_characters: The enquiring author-voice; the critics and reviewers; the cold and self-interested patron; the needy writer of the new age
literary_form: Critical and social dissertation in prose, in numbered sections, in the manner of the comparative enquiry; issued by subscription with printed proposals.
historical_context: It was published in the year before Goldsmith's periodical papers began, as the book trade was expanding, the subscription and the magazine were replacing the patron, and the argument about politeness, commerce and national taste carried on by Shaftesbury, the reviewers and the Scottish societies was becoming an argument about the material fate of authors. Its tone reflects the impoverishment of a recently arrived Irish graduate in Grub Street.
literary_significance: It supplied the classic eighteenth-century statement of the decay of patronage and of the miseries of the professional author, and its survey of European politeness is an early specimen of comparative cultural history written for a general reader. Its complaints are the background to everything Goldsmith later wrote, and its diagnosis was soon taken up by Johnson and by the moralists of the literary marketplace.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work was published with Goldsmith's name and its authorship was never in doubt. The precise dates of composition are not fixed and are left null.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1759, issued on the plan of a subscription and preceded by printed proposals; frequently reprinted and translated, and reprinted among Goldsmith's collected prose. No printer is asserted beyond the 1759 imprint.

title: The Citizen of the World
alternative_titles: The Citizen of the World; or, Letters of a Chinese Philosopher, Respecting His Residence in London
description: Goldsmith's periodical essays cast as the letters of a Chinese philosopher resident in London, first contributed to a daily newspaper and then collected in two volumes. The device of the observing foreigner, familiar from the 'Persian Letters' tradition, is used to make English manners, laws, learning, commerce and show appear strange, and to let a writer of little consequence comment on a great city with the immunity of an outsider.
plot_or_argument: The letters are connected not by plot but by the persona of Lien Chi Altangi, a Chinese merchant-philosopher in London, whose correspondence with friends at home reports and judges everything he meets: the exchange, the playhouse, the auction, the coffee-house and the critics, the luxury of the rich and the misery of the poor, the laws, the duels, the salons and the political factions. His outsider's eye produces the two characteristic effects of the series, an invention of British society as a system of contradictions, and a defence of simple virtue and of the 'mandarins' of his own country against European pretence. As the letters proceed, the philosopher's own family misfortune is woven into the papers, so that the spectators' pleasure is gradually seasoned with sentiment and with a plea for benevolence. Its most quoted material is its account of the 'golden fairies' of British credit, the paper money and the phantom wealth of a commercial nation.
narrative_structure: A sequence of independent periodical letters in two collected volumes, unified by the persona of the Chinese correspondent and by the seasonal and topical round of London life, with a few serial threads, chiefly the philosopher's domestic sorrows, running through.
principal_characters: Lien Chi Altangi, the Chinese philosopher; his correspondent Hoamsy and the family at home; the London citizens, critics, tradesmen and great whom he observes
literary_form: Periodical essay and spectator paper in epistolary form: short papers of character and custom, mixed with fable, translation and reflection, written for a daily newspaper and reprinted as books.
historical_context: It appeared in the efflorescence of the English periodical paper after Addison and Steele, when a contributor could supply a newspaper with a series of essays and when the foreign-letter conceit had become a standard means of criticising national manners. Its publication belongs to the years when Goldsmith was moving between the magazines, the book trade and the great houses, dependent on the very world he describes.
literary_significance: It is the most accomplished of the mid-century spectator series and a central text of the literature of politeness, commerce and national self-observation; its letters shaped the essayistic treatment of commercial society for a generation. It also shows the sentiment of the 1760s turning the essay from a machine of wit into a machine of sympathy.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the papers were known to be Goldsmith's and were collected under his name. Some letters appeared in the newspaper press before the collected edition and were revised for it, so the exact order and dating of individual papers is not fixed here.
bibliographical_notes: First contributed to a London daily newspaper in 1760-61 and collected in two volumes in 1760, with subsequent editions enlarged; reprinted in the standard collections of Goldsmith's works. No printer is asserted beyond the collected imprint of 1760.

title: The Traveller; or, A Prospect of Society
description: Goldsmith's first published poem and the work that established him as a poet: a reflection in heroic couplets on the forms of society and on the place each gives to human happiness, written in the manner of the Augustan philosophical essay in verse and addressed to his friend the painter Sir Joshua Reynolds. It takes the traveller's survey of the nations of Europe as the frame for an argument about happiness, government and contentment.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with the traveller's farewell to his family and his retirement from the world's noise, and proceeds as a survey of the chief states of Europe, each examined for the kind of happiness its institutions secure or refuse. The commercial states of Flanders, the hardy independence of the Swiss cantons, Italy under priestcraft, smiling but servitude-prone Gaul, proud and darkly policed Spain, and England with its liberty, its commerce and its unequal distribution of enjoyments, are each allowed their plea and then judged. The argument is that happiness does not follow from any single form of policy or condition of life, since every state has its own peculiar miseries and every rank its own discontents, and that felicity depends rather on the mind and on the balance of the whole. The close withdraws from the prospect of society to the poet's own retired lot, content to have failed in the world if he has kept his integrity.
narrative_structure: A single sustained argument in the epistle-reflection form: opening retirement and apostrophe, a sequence of national portraits each with its own balance sheet of good and evil, general conclusion on the dependence of happiness on the mind, and personal peroration of retirement.
principal_characters: The traveller-poet and his own family left behind; the nations of Europe as collectively personified conditions of society
literary_form: Philosophical-reflection poem in the tradition of Pope's 'Essay on Man', cast as a verse epistle to a friend and organised as a comparative survey of nations; issued as a separate pamphlet in quarto.
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter, in the polished Augustan manner with balanced antithesis, sententious closure and a good deal of the epigrammatic turn Goldsmith took from Pope.
historical_context: It was composed largely during a country retirement in the English midlands and published at the height of the debate about commercial society, national character and the comparative history of government, in which the Scottish and English moral philosophers were then engaged. Its survey of Europe drew on the Grand Tour and on the travelling literature of the age, and on the post-war confidence and anxiety about British commerce.
literary_significance: It made Goldsmith's poetical reputation at the moment when the couplet tradition was beginning to be questioned, and it remains the best example of the Augustan philosophical survey in verse written in the 1760s. Its doctrine that forms of society do not determine happiness, and its portraits of national character, were much quoted, and it prepared the moral manner of 'The Deserted Village'.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was published anonymously at first but was known and acknowledged as Goldsmith's, and its history is documented in his letters and in the contemporary accounts of its subscription publication.
bibliographical_notes: First printed as a separate poem in 1764, issued on the subscription plan with the author's dedication to Sir Joshua Reynolds; reprinted in the collected poems and often separately. The poem was composed in the years immediately before publication; exact composition dates are not asserted.

title: The Vicar of Wakefield
alternative_titles: The Vicar of Wakefield: A Tale, Supposed to be Written by Himself
description: Goldsmith's novel, and one of the most read and most translated prose fictions of the century: the story of the family of Dr Primrose, a country chaplain, reduced from competence to poverty and tried by a succession of calamities, which it narrates in the first person with an unaffected and comic seriousness. It is the exemplary domestic and sentimental novel of the 1760s, and its fame has rested ever since on the question of whether its virtue is sincere or merely naive.
plot_or_argument: The Primroses, happy and prosperous in their parish, lose their fortune when a trust in which their savings were lodged fails, and they retire to a smaller house where the family's learning, vanity and simplicity are displayed in the father's sermons and in the accomplishments of the daughters. Squire Thornhill, the dissolute nephew of a local great man, seduces and abandons the elder daughter Olivia, while the younger Arabella is courted in turn; the father's resentful attempt at revenge by letter ruins him further, and the family is reduced to a jail in which the father's philosophy, the mother's indignation and the children's several fates are all tested. A disguised benefactor, appearing as the humble Mr Burchell, is revealed at the close as the real power who has been testing them throughout, and the novel ends with restitution, recovered fortune and marriage. The movement is thus from prosperity through a series of calamities to a providential restoration, with patience and benevolence as the family's governing virtues.
narrative_structure: A picaresque-sentimental novel in fifty-two short chapters, told in the first person by the vicar, with a continuous linear sequence of prosperity, fall, trial and restoration, and with the narrator's own simplicity as the source of the comedy.
principal_characters: Dr Primrose, the vicar; his wife; Olivia and Arabella; Moses and Dicky; Squire Thornhill; the disguised benefactor Mr Burchell; the gaoler and the minor friends of the family
literary_form: Sentimental and domestic novel in the picaresque line, in short numbered chapters, with the first-person narrative of an amiable patriarch; mixed comedy and pathos, with inserted songs and moral reflection.
historical_context: It appeared in the decade of the sentimental comedy and of Richardson's moral fiction, when the novel was being taken up as an instrument of instruction and when the 'good-natur'd' philosophy of the moral sense school was a subject of public debate. It was published at a stroke by a writer otherwise known as a poet, essayist and hack, and its scene of rural retirement speaks for an age anxious about the decay of the country and of the paternal clergyman.
literary_significance: It is one of the two or three novels that fixed the sentimental domestic form for later generations, and its portrait of family virtue under trial was admired and ridiculed in equal measure, the most durable of the ridicule being Samuel Johnson's objection that its whole design sacrificed probability to affecting circumstance. Its influence on the country-pastoral novel, on the fiction of trials and providential restoration, and on the nineteenth-century reading of Goldsmith as a man of feeling, is considerable.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the novel was published with Goldsmith's name, and its sale to the trade was famously negotiated for him by Samuel Johnson. Disputed questions concern the order of composition and the extent of revision, not the authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1766 in two volumes; reprinted extremely widely in the following decades, in editions sometimes revised, abridged and adapted, and translated into the principal European languages. No printer is asserted beyond the 1766 imprint.

title: The Good-Natur'd Man
description: Oliver Goldsmith's first produced comedy, and the play with which he entered the quarrel about sentimental comedy: an essay in the 'laughing comedy' of which he became the theorist, in which goodness of disposition, not wit or contrivance, is made the subject and the instrument of the plot. Its unhappy first run gave it a place in theatrical history larger than its later performance on the stage would suggest.
plot_or_argument: The comedy is built on a generous young man whose very openness of temper makes him the prey of everyone with a claim upon him, and on the confusions his readiness to oblige produces in his own affairs of the heart. He is in love with a lady under the control of an interested guardian, and the artful about him exploit his good nature in order to advance their own designs, so that the action consists less of a scheme than of a series of impositions.
