Against these the play sets the worth of uncalculated kindness, and its resolution restores the lovers and exposes the designs. The moral interest is deliberately affective rather than satirical: the audience is asked to laugh with good humour and to approve benevolence, and the antipathy of the malicious and the calculating is what the comedy finally defeats.
narrative_structure: A five-act comedy of character and imposition, with a double amatory plot and a succession of deceptions worked upon the protagonist's generosity, resolved by exposure and restitution.
principal_characters: The good-natur'd young lover at its centre; the lady he loves and the guardian who controls her; the artful claimants upon his generosity; his friends and dependants
literary_form: Comedy in five acts, in dialogue prose with sententious and tender passages, written for the London stage in the reforming 1760s and prefaced in print by epistle and dramatis personae.
historical_context: It belongs to the theatrical controversy of the 1760s between the laughing comedy of manners and feeing and the sentimental comedy of distress, a debate Goldsmith had already entered as a critic and was to state formally in his essay on the theatre, which argued for laughing against sentimental comedy. It was produced in the season when the managers were remaking the repertoire and when the 'sentimental' piece was at its height.
literary_significance: It is the first of the two plays in which Goldsmith tried to restore mirth and national character to the English stage against the fashion for distress, and its failure and its defence shaped the subsequent history of the sentimental-comedy quarrel. It supplies the practical counterpart to his theoretical case for laughing comedy.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the play is Goldsmith's and its production is documented. The dating of the surviving manuscript and the extent of the revisions made after the first run are matters of editorial detail, not of authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First performed in London and first printed in 1768; the printed text follows the stage and the play was revived and reprinted in later seasons and in the collected editions of Goldsmith's works.

title: The Deserted Village
description: Goldsmith's most admired poem and one of the canonical complaints of English literature: the elegy of a ruined country village, remembered as the seat of poverty, pleasure and paternal virtue and now deserted through the accumulation of wealth. Its remembered place is Auburn, an imagined Irish village drawn from the scene of the poet's own childhood, and its argument is a moral history of the decay of the countryside.
plot_or_argument: The poem moves from the present desolation of the village to the loving inventory of what has been lost: its sports, its fireside, its church and school, its poor and their pleasures. The portraits that follow, the pedlar, the schoolmistress, the minister and the beggar-woman, are a social survey of a community now scattered, and the poem then turns the survey into an argument about causes. Luxury, the love of gain, the enclosure and the pooling of landed property in great hands, and the pride of the rich are indicted as the forces that have expelled the peasantry, so that the village's desertion becomes the emblem of a national disease in which population and virtue are exchanged for wealth. The emigration of the ruined poor to the colonies supplies the poem's saddest consequence, and the closing movement retires to the poet's own lot, content to have preserved feeling and integrity in an age of opulence.
narrative_structure: A continuous elegiac-complaint poem in the manner of a topographical meditation: present desolation, remembered scenes and characters, analysis of causes, prospect of emigration and moral conclusion in the poet's own retirement.
principal_characters: The deserted village of Auburn and its scattered poor; the pedlar; the schoolmistress; the minister; the emigrants; the rich and their accumulations
literary_form: Elegiac and didactic poem in the estate-and-topographical tradition, in heroic couplets, with the personification of luxury and the social portrait borrowed from the descriptive tradition; issued as a separate quarto.
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter, in a plain, sententious and affective manner, with the balanced generalisation of the Augustan school used for complaint rather than for wit.
historical_context: It appeared in the early 1770s, in the middle of the public debate about depopulation, engrossment and enclosure, and after the famine and emigration which had made Irish decay an English question. Its politics belong with the country-party language of liberty and corruption and with the moral economists' alarm at luxury, and it was attacked at least one reviewer for its doctrine rather than for its verse.
literary_significance: It is the great poem of rural depopulation and of the sentimental critique of commercial society, and it fixed the image of the lost village in English and Irish consciousness. Its influence on later rural poetry, on the literature of the cleared Highlands and of enclosure, and on the language of anti-luxury is considerable, and it established Goldsmith's reputation as the poet of feeling.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published anonymously at first but immediately known and acknowledged as Goldsmith's, and his authorship was never in question. The poem's chronology of composition, which stretched over several years and was revised after publication, is not fixed here.
bibliographical_notes: First printed separately in 1770, with dedication to Sir Joshua Reynolds, and reprinted in the collected poems with revisions; many later editions, school texts and translations, and several contemporary replies in prose and verse were occasioned by its politics. No printer is asserted beyond the 1770 imprint.

title: She Stoops to Conquer; or, The Mistakes of a Night
description: Goldsmith's masterpiece for the stage and one of the two or three comedies that survived continuously in the English repertory from the eighteenth century: a laughing comedy in which a mistake about the identity of a house sets the whole plot going and in which a young woman deliberately 'stoops' in order to win the man she loves. It was written in explicit opposition to the sentimental comedy of distress and was dedicated to Samuel Johnson.
plot_or_argument: Young Marlow, ardent and forward with women of easy reputation but dumb and bashful before a modest woman, is brought by his father's arrangement to the house of the neighbouring Mr Hardcastle, whom he is to marry. The idler Tony Lumpkin, who has no wish to be married himself and delights in mischief, directs the travellers to Hardcastle's house as though it were an inn; Hardcastle, learning of the mistake and determined to cure his son's bashfulness by it, plays the landlord. Marlow therefore behaves with insolent freedom towards the real daughter of the house, whom he takes for a barmaid, and Kate, perceiving what has happened, consents to the deception and 'stoops' to the character in order to be loved for herself. The subplots of Tony's own refused match and of the elopements are gathered into the same night's confusion, and the discovery of the mistake at the end restores order, consent and the couple.
narrative_structure: A five-act comedy of errors and disguised identities with a single night's duration, driven by one sustained mistake and by characters' knowledge of it, and resolved by the discovery scene; the amatory main plot is supported by the comic country plot of the idler and his intended.
principal_characters: Young Marlow; Kate Hardcastle; Mr Hardcastle; Mrs Hardcastle; Tony Lumpkin; Mr Hastings; Constance Neville
literary_form: Laughing comedy in five acts, dialogue prose, for the London theatre, printed with prologue and epilogue and with the customary dramatis personae; built on the comic conceits of mistaken place and assumed condition.
historical_context: It was produced in the season in which the managers were rebuilding the comedy of the London stage and in which Goldsmith's quarrel with the theatre of sentimental distress had been running for years; its success is part of the theatrical regeneration associated with the great players and managers of the 1770s. Its satire upon provincial idleness and upon the fashionable manners of London belongs to the same decade's comedy of national character.
literary_significance: It is the most durable English comedy between Congreve and Sheridan, and the practical vindication of Goldsmith's theory that comedy should correct by laughter rather than by distress. Its Tony Lumpkin and its Kate Hardcastle became standards of the repertory, and its plot of the assumed condition remains the best-known illustration of the eighteenth-century effort to reconcile sentiment with mirth.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the play is Goldsmith's, its production history is documented, and the printed edition carries his name and his dedication. Its relation to the earlier project of 'The Mistakes of a Night' is a matter of editorial chronology rather than of authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First performed in London and first printed in 1773, with the prologue spoken on the opening night and with the dedication to Samuel Johnson; reprinted in the collected dramatic works and continuously in the repertory. No printer is asserted beyond the 1773 imprint.

title: Song to David
description: Christopher Smart's great ode, a poem of praise addressed to the psalmist-king and through him to God, and the most extraordinary achievement of English Augustan verse between the odes of Dryden and those of the Romantic period. It passes from the invitation to sing to the works and the names of David, to music, to the beasts and elements attending him, and finally to the typological and prophetic range of the Israelite kingdom. Its stanzas are irregular by design, each shaped to its subject, and its diction, rhyme and vowel-pattern are among the most carefully experimental of the century.
plot_or_argument: The poem is an invitation, a catalogue and a praise. It begins by calling the muse of Israel to her task and then proceeds through the parts of David's story and his attributes, treating the psalmist as the inventor and patron of sacred music and as the type of Christ. The middle movements are a natural history and a physics of praise: harp and organ, the vocal powers of beasts, birds and the elements, and the famous enquiry into the properties of vowels and consonants, in which Smart's theory of the inherent music of language is made the ground of the poem's own practice. The conclusion gathers the typology together, making David's kingdom and the builder of the temple figures of a spiritual and prophetic order. Praise, not narrative, is the argument, and the poem's form is an argument that variety of measure is itself a mode of devotion.
narrative_structure: A continuous ode in unequal stanzas, moving by association and amplification from invocation through the subjects of David's praise to typological and prophetic conclusion; the stanzaic irregularity is planned, not accidental.
principal_characters: David, the psalmist and king, addressed and celebrated; the personified muse and music; the created things, animal, vegetable and elemental, that attend the praise
literary_form: Sacred ode or hymn of praise in the English Pindaric tradition as revised in the eighteenth century, with stanzaic response to the order of the subject and with a strongly Hebraic rhetoric of accumulation and parallelism.
meter_and_prosody: A planned variety of measures: long and short lines, recurring burden-like refrains, dense internal and vowel rhyme, and experiments in the sound of the alphabet itself; the poem is the age's most self-conscious treatment of the relation of phonetic material to devotion.
historical_context: It was published in the year of Smart's release from the retirement in which he had been confined, and stands with 'Jubilate Agno' and the other poems of the confinement years at the centre of his work. Its Hebraism belongs to an age of psalm translation, of the debate about 'enthusiasm' and true religious poetry, and of the High-Church and Jacobite sympathies of its author.
literary_significance: It is the supreme religious ode of the mid-eighteenth century and the strongest claim made in the period for poetry as an act of praise rather than of instruction or of taste; its recovery in the twentieth century altered the estimation of Smart and of Augustan verse generally. Samuel Johnson's recorded admiration of parts of it is the beginning of its reputation among the poets of the club.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem is Smart's and its authorship was never disputed. The year of first printing is recorded, but the venue of the first impression and the stages of composition within the confinement years are matters of editorial detail which are not asserted here.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1763; the text was reprinted in the collections of Smart's poems issued after his death and in the scholarly editions of the twentieth century, which also established the relation between the printed poem and the manuscript drafts. No printer or periodical is asserted for the first impression.

title: A Jubilate Agno
description: Christopher Smart's immense poem of universal rejoicing, written during his years of confinement and retirement and not printed in his lifetime. It is structured as a responsive sequence of pairs, each joining some creature, object or abstraction to another in the duty of praising God, and it expands from the animal kingdom to the alphabet, to the languages of the world, to the poet's own person and history. Its mixture of theology, natural history, philology and autobiography is without analogue in English verse.
plot_or_argument: There is no narrative, only an enormous act of doxology. The poem proceeds in responsive pairs, in which a member of creation is set to rejoice with another, and it passes through cats, dogs, birds, insects, the elements, the parts of the body, the letters, the tongues ancient and modern, and the institutions and professions of men. The governing argument is that all being is under an obligation to praise, and that the poet, whose own case and wrongs are repeatedly pleaded in the middle of the doxology, stands as an example of the created thing that refuses or is unable to complete its part. The effect is at once encyclopaedic and intensely personal, and the poem's logic is that of a litany rather than of a discourse.
narrative_structure: A continuous responsive sequence in paired half-lines, with the response of the priest and the people marked, broken into sections by the change of subject and by the poet's intrusive personal passages; no closure was supplied by the author.
principal_characters: The Creator addressed and praised; the whole catalogue of creatures, letters and languages; the poet's own self, 'for I' clauses of defence and complaint
literary_form: Devotional and encyclopaedic poem in responsive measure, related to the litany, to the psalms and to the hymn; surviving in author's manuscript and unprinted for two centuries.
meter_and_prosody: The pair-verse of the poem: a long line divided by a caesura into two responding parts, with the reiterated formulas 'for' and 'let ... rejoice with ...', producing a prosody of parallelism and accumulation closer to Hebrew and to chant than to any Augustan measure.
historical_context: It was composed during the poet's confinement, the same period that produced the 'Song to David' and the other poems of the retirement, and it belongs to the culture of enthusiasm, religious melancholy and psalm-praise which the Augustan public found so difficult to classify. Its survival in manuscript made it a twentieth-century discovery, and its publication changed the terms of Smart's reputation.
literary_significance: It is one of the few entirely original large forms created in English religious poetry, and its recovery established Smart as a central rather than eccentric figure of Augustan letters; its prosody, its catalogue method and its fusion of natural history with praise anticipate much later poetry. It is also the principal document of the age's quarrel between enthusiasm and reason.
attribution_notes: Attribution to Smart is unquestioned; the difficulty is bibliographical, not authorial. The poem survived only in his manuscript and was not printed in the eighteenth century, so no publication year can be recorded and the field is left null; the composition years are given as the span of the confinement, which is the accepted but not precisely dated account.
bibliographical_notes: Composed in manuscript during the years of confinement and preserved in Smart's own hand; extracts and partial printings came much later and the complete text was first published in the twentieth century in a scholarly edition from the manuscript. Because the first full print lies outside the period of this installment, the publication field is recorded as null.

title: Hymns for the Feasts of the Church
description: Smart's devotional hymns for the seasons and principal feasts of the Christian year, belonging to the liturgical side of his work and to the same religious imagination as the 'Song to David' and 'Jubilate Agno'. They were written for the uses of the church calendar rather than for the poetical market, and they survive outside any lifetime collection of his verse.
plot_or_argument: The hymns take the anniversaries and offices of the church year as their occasions, and each is built upon the scriptural and typological material proper to its feast. Their argument is not doctrinal but doxological: the year is presented as a sequence of mercies and manifestations, and the worshipper is taught to rejoice in each in its order. As in the longer poems, the concrete and the created world is pressed into service as the imagery of praise, and the personal voice of the poet is subdued to the demands of a congregation's utterance.
narrative_structure: A cycle of independent liturgical hymns arranged by the feasts and seasons of the church year, with no continuous narrative and with the calendar supplying the order.
principal_characters: The worshipping church addressed and instructing itself; the persons and events of scripture invoked at each feast
literary_form: Hymn-cycle for the liturgical year, in the tradition of the paraphrase and of the church-meter hymn, with the poet's characteristic Hebraic and typological diction; the pieces are short, strophic and singable.
meter_and_prosody: Hymn measures of the common and long metre types, with the plain, accented and heavily parallelist phrasing Smart used for devotional verse; the stanzas are regular, in contrast with the experimental measures of his odes.
historical_context: They belong to the religious culture of Smart's later years, in which hymn-writing for the church year was a work of party and of devotion, between the Latitudinarian and the evangelical and High-Church traditions. The same decade saw the great flowering of English hymnody by Watts, Doddridge and the Wesleys, against which Smart's church-year hymns assert an older and more liturgical model.
literary_significance: They complete the picture of Smart as a poet of the prayer book and the psalms rather than of the magazine, and they are the least Augustan of his verse in their intention to be sung by a congregation. Their survival outside print in his lifetime is part of the history of his neglect.
attribution_notes: Attribution to Smart is not contested; what cannot be settled here is their chronology and their first publication, since the cycle was not issued as a book in his lifetime and the separate hymns have complicated reprinting histories. The year fields are therefore left null rather than estimated.
bibliographical_notes: Composed for the offices and feasts of the church and transmitted in manuscript and in later collections of Smart's devotional verse; the posthumous collections and the scholarly editions of the twentieth century carry the text. No first-print year is asserted here.
